conversation.content:
Hello there, I’m Dr. M—one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk today; I know the early weeks with a new baby can feel like a whirl-wind.

I’d like to do a quick check-in with you using the Edinburgh Postpartum/Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way to see how we can best support you.

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through one question at a time—no hurry, no pressure. When you’re ready, we can begin.

Question 1: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things? If so, how much of the time—always, sometimes, not very often, or never?
Mostly sometimes, I’d say. I can still laugh when my husband cracks a joke or when the baby makes a silly face, but it feels kind of muted—like the laughter doesn’t last as long as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… like I said, I can laugh, but it’s only sometimes, and even when I do, it feels kind of flat—like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over or taking the baby for a walk—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it was before. It feels more like “I guess that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the hours.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding him right or I did something during the day to mess up his routine. I know it’s probably not rational, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. I’ll suddenly wonder if he’s breathing okay in the middle of the night, or I’ll worry that a tiny rash means something awful. It doesn’t last long—usually I can talk myself down—but it still feels like I’m on edge for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick rush of “what-if” when I hear him make a weird noise or when I’m alone with him at night. My heart speeds up for a minute, but it passes before I get truly scared.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some of the time. There are moments—like when he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up—when I feel a bit swamped. I usually manage to get through it, but it feels harder than it should, like I’m walking through thick air.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I do have trouble drifting off once or twice a week, but it’s more from running to-do lists in my head than from feeling really unhappy. Once I’m asleep I stay asleep—unless the baby wakes me, of course.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’d say yes, sometimes. Most of the day I’m okay, but there are stretches—especially in the late afternoon when I’m tired—where I just feel kind of down and weepy. It’s not all day, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried… maybe once or twice this week. It’s not that I’m sobbing all day—just that sudden wave of “I can’t do this” when the baby’s fussy and I’m exhausted. The tears come for a few minutes, then I wipe them off and keep going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired and a little overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant 3–4 wks)

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):  
- Anhedonia: diminished pleasure/enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Generalized & infant-focused anxiety, nocturnal hyper-vigilance (Q4, Q5)  
- Intermittent low mood, late-day tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Episodic feeling “swamped” or “walking through thick air” (Q6)  
- Occasional initial insomnia related to mental over-activity (Q7)  

Denies: persistent anhedonia, daily crying, panic attacks, self-harm ideation (Q10).

Pattern: Sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms, situational triggers (fatigue, infant crying), no safety concerns identified.

Screening significance:  
Mild to moderate mood/anxiety symptoms consistent with postpartum stress; fall below threshold for major depression but warrant close monitoring, psycho-education, and re-screen in 2 weeks.
